cells.tense: The cycle has closed and the hands are still steady on what comes next.
cells.ask: Tell the person beside you that one thing of theirs is done and good — then stay quiet and let them decide what happens to it. The closing was yours to do; the next move is theirs.
cells.core:
You get to the end of things on purpose and then let go. A project lands, a stretch of caring finds its shape, something you raised is standing on its own — and you're still willing to stand near it without managing what it does next. That's the rare part. Most people either stop the thing before it finishes or grip it after.

So the real work here is keeping the door open. The cycle closes and you let the next one arrive at its own pace — you don't go looking for what the ending should mean, and you don't take the ending back. That steady way of finishing is doing quiet work, sending what you've finished off into hands other than yours. It's what makes people trust you with things that are still growing.
cells.sheetLine: You finish things on purpose, then leave the door open.
cells.verb: integrating what's finished and handing it forward
cells.place: where what is growing is tended

cells.tense: The ending has already happened in the head, and the hands are running ahead to catch up with it.
cells.ask: Pick the thing you're pushing and hold it three more days. Write down one thing it still needs that you'd rather skip past. Then let the third day end without finishing it — if you can.
cells.core:
You've already decided how this ends, and you're steering everything toward that ending. The growing thing in front of you gets hurried, its loose ends tied before you've looked at them, people praised for progress they haven't made — because an open middle is harder to sit in than a done thing.

That's what the push is doing. It's not that you don't care; it's that you care so much you'd rather have it finished than let it take its own time. But a thing finished early isn't finished. It's just out of your sight, and the part you skipped is still owed, by whoever comes next. Three days won't hurt it. They might show you what your rush has been costing.
cells.sheetLine: You keep finishing things before they're done.

cells.tense: A completion is standing behind the person, and the hands are still working the gate as if nothing ever got through it.
cells.ask: Take one thing you've kept going — a draft, a good habit, a half-built arrangement — and hand it over as done. Clearly and plainly to someone who'll use it. Then let it be theirs.
cells.core:
You're standing at a gate that already opened. Things you raised have arrived — someone you cared for is steady, work you finished sits completed somewhere — and you're still treating it as unfinished, as if more care will finish the job. So you keep the gate shut and keep working, and pull the next thing and the next one in behind you.

It keeps you busy at a door that's behind you now. Letting something close isn't the same as abandoning it. Handing it over, clearly and for good, is what tells your own body the work is done. The appetite for the next arrival is good. It just needs a finished thing under it instead of an open one.

cells.tense: Things are being released already, and no one has told the one doing the releasing.
cells.ask: Name one thing you've already let go of, out loud. No wondering whether it was the right call. Just the fact of it, said where someone can hear you, and then move on to what's next.
cells.core:
You're letting things go without much noticing you've done it. You put down the argument, you hand the child off, you stop watering something and don't call it a decision — and then you talk as if that hand were still holding it, still responsible for whether it grows.

Some endings already happened in your care, quietly, on their own. Calling one of them yours — not as a loss, as a release — clears the fog. Holding on wasn't doing the growing anyway. When you can say what's finished, the next thing shows up without you having to hunt for it, and you meet it with hands that are actually free.
cells.sheetLine: You've let go already. Start calling it that.
cells.verb: integrating what's finished and handing it forward

attempts.check: The unsupported claim I nearly made: reading the person's history behind the gate — saying when they stopped letting things finish, or that a particular loss taught it. The record says only that a capacity is past-anchored, not what put it there; a reader holding a newborn, a manuscript, or a body of their own work could reasonably say the gate isn't theirs, that things do close for them, that the endless seeking lives in one room only. So the Too Little cell stays on the gate and what stands past it and never says what happened there or how long. The ask, hand one finished thing to someone who'll actually use it, survives being wrong — it asks the person to act, not to agree with me — and it's narrower than the record alone would license. The sentence that serves me more than them, cut from the Too Much draft: 'you already know how this ends' — that's me being prescient, not describing something they could watch happening. That draft says what they push instead.
